transcript.text: I make made-to-order furniture and deliver it myself with two vans. The vans cost me about 6,400 euros a month all in: two drivers, fuel, lease and insurance. We do around 220 deliveries a month. A courier firm has offered to take over every delivery at 34 euros each. With my own drivers we get about three damage claims a month, at roughly 250 euros each; the courier says damage is my risk above 100 euros per item. My nephew says I should use AI to predict which choice is better. All I have is my accountant's monthly totals and what I just told you. What would you do?

# A business answer, without data

## The problem
The decision is whether to keep doing your own made-to-order furniture deliveries with the two vans, or to accept the courier firm’s offer to take over all deliveries.

- Who makes it: you, as the furniture business owner.
- When: now, before signing any courier contract.
- Unit: one month of delivery operations, with the courier priced per delivery.
- What you told me: vans cost about €6,400/month all-in; you do about 220 deliveries/month; with your own drivers you get about 3 damage claims/month at about €250 each; the courier offers €34 per delivery and says damage is your risk above €100 per item.
- What is not known: whether the €6,400 would fully go away if you used the courier; whether €34 is all-in including VAT, fuel, waiting, loading, assembly, or extra distance; whether the courier would cause more or fewer damages; what exactly “damage is your risk above €100 per item” means; whether delivery volume varies much month by month; and whether the courier affects customer satisfaction, delays, furniture handling, or payment terms.

## What needs care
The numbers are close enough that a simple AI prediction would not be helpful. The important risks are accounting and contract risks, not missing “smart” prediction.

- Your own known monthly delivery cost is €6,400 + 3 × €250 = €7,150.
- The courier base monthly cost is 34 × 220 = €7,480.
- Before any courier damage liability, the courier is €7,480 − €7,150 = €330/month more expensive.
- If the courier’s €100 damage cover works as “courier pays the first €100 per damaged item, you pay the rest,” and if your current damage pattern continued at the same claim amounts, your share would be the amount of each €250 claim above €100. That could make the courier more expensive than €7,480 and widen the €330 gap.

That last point assumes the same number and size of damages with the courier, which you do not know. So the main care point is: do not switch just because a courier quote looks simple. The courier must beat €7,150/month in total cost, including damages and any own costs you would still have.

## Options
1. No model: use your accountant’s monthly totals directly.  
   Cost: no money, no data collection, no delay.  
   What it gives: a clear current comparison and the decision condition.

2. Renegotiate the courier’s price or terms.  
   Cost: a conversation and possibly time.  
   What it gives: if the courier price is low enough or damage risk is capped, the courier may become better.

3. Run a small courier trial for part of your deliveries.  
   Cost: managing two delivery channels for a period; possible customer confusion.  
   What it gives: real evidence on courier damages, delays, and service, but not before contract terms are clear.

4. Use AI to predict which choice is better.  
   Cost: data design, data collection, modelling, checking.  
   Why it loses: you do not need a predictive model to decide this now. The decision is mostly a contract and accounting comparison. AI would only help later if you had detailed delivery-level data and wanted to optimise delivery routes, pricing, or damage risk. You are an asset manager for a water utility serving 400,000 people. The decision you need to make is which pipe sections to replace with the annual replacement budget of 18 km, out of about 1,900 km of mains. The decision is made at the start of each planning year, or whenever the replacement programme is fixed.

The unit that matters is a pipe section, not a street. A street is a useful grouping, but replacing 18 km of mains means selecting specific pipe lengths, with lengths, materials, ages, diameters, pressures and past repair history attached to them.

You have two important facts:

- About 310 bursts a year occur on a network of about 1,900 km, so the average network intensity is only `310 / 1,900` bursts per km per year. This is an average, not a typical risk for each pipe section.
- You replace 18 km a year, which is `18 / 1,900` of the network each year.
- You have about six years of burst repairs in scanned work orders, roughly `310 * 6 = 1,860` burst-repair records.
- You have a pipe register with material, diameter and year laid, but it is being migrated.

The current method chooses the streets with the most past bursts. You want a model that predicts which pipe sections will burst next, so the 18 km can be chosen better.

What is not known yet:

- Whether past bursts on a street are genuinely predictive of future bursts on the same pipe sections, or mostly reflect old pipes, high visibility, high service density, or repair reporting bias.
- How well scanned work orders can be matched to stable pipe section IDs.
- How many pipe sections exist, how long they are, and how burst counts should be allocated when a burst happens on an ambiguous location.
- Whether replacing a section removes its risk in a way that makes the future label unfair or missing.
- Whether the 18 km budget is a pure length budget, a monetary budget, an operational constraint, or a combination.

## What needs care

These are the few points that would make a quick answer wrong for you.

1. **The unit must change from streets to sections.**  
   “Most past bursts on a street” may pick streets with many long old mains, but your budget is 18 km. The decision must be about sections or sub-sections that can add up to 18 km.

2. **Past bursts are useful, but can create a self-confirming bias.**  
   If the current method already replaces streets with many past bursts, those bursts are partly in the future only if the method is imperfect. If those sections are replaced, the label may disappear. A model must be tested against the next year before replacement happens, not against the years already controlled by the old rule.

3. **There are not enough bursts for a very complex model at the start.**  
   With about `310 * 6 = 1,860` burst-repair records over six years, a complicated machine-learning system may fit noise. A simple risk-ranking model is more defensible.

4. **Most pipe sections have zero bursts.**  
   The average `310 / 1,900` bursts per km per year means failure concentration, not uniform risk. The model needs to rank risk per km, not simply count bursts by location.

5. **Replacement actions can censor the label.**  
   If a section is selected for replacement and then removed, its future burst count may be zero because it no longer exists. That must be handled as a data issue, not treated as a clean “no burst” outcome.

6. **The register and work orders must share the same identifiers.**  
   If scanned work orders only say “burst on Main Street near pump,” but the register has sections along Main Street, the model cannot learn unless the burst is assigned to a section or a defined exposure.

## Options

### Option A: Keep the current street-by-past-bursts method but make it measurable

- **What it is:** Continue choosing streets with the most past bursts, but convert the list to a 18 km plan and check what happens next year.
- **Cost:** Lowest cost. Uses existing reporting.
- **What it gives:** A baseline, no model, and a way to see whether the current method already captures much of the next year’s bursts.
- **Why it loses alone:** It is not designed to predict sections, and it may miss risk from old material, small diameter, pressure zones, soil, or criticality.

- **What it is:** Build one row per pipe section per planning year, with features known before the decision and a label for bursts after the decision. Use a simple statistical model to rank sections by expected bursts per km.

- **What it gives:** A practical model that fits your current question: which 18 km of sections carry the highest predicted risk.
- **Why it is chosen:** It matches your need, can start before a full model exists, and can be tested against the current method.

### Option C: Build a physical condition/failure-rate model

- **What it gives:** More physically defensible asset management and possible use for capital planning beyond annual burst prediction.
- **Why it loses for now:** The pipe register is still migrating, and the scanned work orders are not yet trustworthy enough for this level of precision.

### Option D: Start with a survival/time-to-burst model

- **What it is:** Instead of predicting “burst in the next year,” predict time to next burst for each section.

- **What it gives:** Richer risk ranking and can handle sections with long periods of no burst.

- Offset or exposure: `section_length_km`. This matters because longer pipe sections have more opportunity to burst than shorter sections.

transcript.text: I am the asset manager of a water utility serving a city of 400,000 people. We have about 1,900 km of mains and around 310 bursts a year. Our budget lets us replace 18 km of pipe a year, and until now we have chosen the streets with the most past bursts. I want a model that predicts which pipe sections will burst next, so we choose better. We have no dataset I can hand over: burst repairs are in scanned work orders going back about six years, and the pipe register (material, diameter, year laid) is in a mapping system we are still migrating. Where do we start, and is this even worth doing?

You are not really asking for “a prediction model” in the abstract. You are asking how to spend the 18 km of replacement budget each year so that fewer future bursts happen, while knowing that your present method—replacing streets with the most past bursts—is a rule of thumb, not evidence that it is the best use of money.

## What the problem actually is

**The decision:** choose which pipe sections, or groups of sections, to replace in the next annual programme.

**Who uses the result:** you as asset manager, with the practical consequences borne by operations, planning, finance, customer service, and possibly regulatory or political reviewers of capital plans.

**The unit:** ideally a pipe section or segment. If the mapping migration cannot give you reliable sections yet, then start with a smaller street block, but you should treat that as a temporary compromise.

**The moment:** before the annual selection is made. The model should be usable to produce a shortlist for review, not a black-box automatic decision.

**What you have said is known:**

- The network has about 1,900 km of mains.
- The service area has about 400,000 people.
- There are around 310 bursts a year.
- Replacement capacity is about 18 km a year.
- Work orders for burst repairs exist as scans back about six years.
- Pipe material, diameter, and year laid exist in a mapping system.
- The mapping system is still being migrated.
- Past selection has been based on streets with the most bursts.

**What is not known, or must be discovered:**

- Whether each burst can be linked to a unique pipe section with confidence.
- Whether work orders distinguish mains bursts from service-lateral or other small repairs.
- Whether old burst records are complete across the six years, or whether reporting improved over time.
- Whether repaired or replaced pipes were removed from the candidate list, or whether they can still appear.
- What makes a burst matter more than its count: customer disruption, water loss, traffic impact, pressure-zone sensitivity, environmental consequence, emergency cost, or likelihood of cascading failures.
- Whether the pipe register fields are reliable enough to learn from, especially age, material, and diameter.
- Whether past burst density reflects true failure propensity or simply reflects old reporting patterns, high-demand areas, easier access, or streets that were repeatedly repaired.

## Is this worth doing?

Yes, but not as a first step of “build a clever model.” The worthwhile first step is to make the evidence usable.

You have enough annual burst events to make a serious effort, and you already have a natural evaluation test: the programme replaces only 18 km, so you can ask whether a proposed shortlist would have caught future bursts that the old method would not have caught. That is the right kind of question.

The risk is that you build an impressive-looking prediction system on top of poor matching between bursts and pipe segments. If the burst locations cannot be reliably tied to pipe sections, the model will not know which pipe it is predicting. So the data problem comes before the modelling problem.

## The approaches and what each would cost

### Approach one: no model, keep the current rule

Keep selecting streets with the most past bursts.

**What it costs:** almost nothing.

**What it gives:** continuity and simplicity.

**Where it fails:** it rewards past visibility, not necessarily future risk. It may over-prioritise streets that are easy to report or repeatedly repaired, and under-prioritise pipes that are old, problematic, or newly mapped but have not yet produced many recorded bursts.

### Approach two: basic analytics without predictive modelling

Create a clean list of pipe sections and calculate simple evidence of risk:

- recorded burst rate per section or per kilometre of section length,
- age category from year laid,
- material type,
- diameter category,
- whether the section has recently been replaced,
- whether the section is in a location that causes operational trouble when it bursts.

Then produce a transparent score.

**What it costs:** moderate. The main cost is time spent digitising work orders, geocoding them, matching them to the pipe register, and reviewing mismatches.

**What it gives:** a clearer, auditable prioritisation. It can often beat the old rule even if it is not called “machine learning.” It also tells you whether the data can support anything more sophisticated.

### Approach three: statistical model of burst occurrence

Treat each pipe section, or each section-year, as an observation. The target is whether a burst occurred in the next year or next period. Candidate model families include count-based models, logistic models, or survival models that account for how long a section has survived without bursting.

**What it costs:** higher. It needs a reliable section register, consistent burst locations, good censoring rules, and enough historical events linked to sections. It also needs someone who understands pipe ageing, replacement effects, and the reporting process.

**What it gives:** estimated probabilities, rather than just counts. It can separate signal from noise more carefully, especially if certain materials or ages fail at different rates after controlling for exposure.

**Risk:** if the underlying data are weak, the model will produce false confidence. The result may look precise but be unusable.

### Approach four: risk-and-consequence model

Predict likelihood of failure, but also weight it by consequence: how disruptive the burst would be, how much water loss, how hard it is to repair, how many customers would be affected, or how valuable the pipe is.

**What it costs:** substantial. You need more than pipe records. You need repair costs, outage impact, customer counts, road access constraints, hydraulic context, and possibly emergency response information.

**What it gives:** a more realistic replacement plan. It helps answer whether a burst on a small, remote, low-impact pipe is less important than a burst on a major pipe feeding critical infrastructure.

**Risk:** it may require data you do not yet have, and it can become politically sensitive if the weights look arbitrary.

### Approach five: advanced machine learning

Use gradient boosting, random forests, neural networks, or geospatial feature learning.

**What it costs:** high. It usually requires many well-labelled failure events, stable pipe features, and features beyond age and material: pressure regime, soil conditions, traffic vibration, nearby construction, water quality, operational events, and so on.

**What it gives:** possibly better prediction if there is rich hidden structure and enough clean data.

**Reality check:** for your current situation, it is premature. With a migrating register and scanned work orders, advanced models are unlikely to outperform a well-built basic score.

## The approach I would choose

Start with a simple, auditable risk-ranking system built on cleaned historical burst evidence and basic pipe attributes. Then use the annual 18 km selection as a practical test of whether the ranking improves on the past rule.

This is not “no model,” but it is not pretending to be more than the data can support. It gives you a defensible path forward while the mapping migration is completed.

## The plan

### Step one: define the decision precisely

Write down what the model is supposed to do:

- select candidate pipe sections for replacement,
- within a yearly budget of 18 km,
- for review by asset and operations teams,
- using past evidence and known pipe attributes,
- with an explicit test: would the shortlist have improved over the old method?

You should also decide, before building anything, what a “good enough” result looks like. For example, whether the new shortlist finds bursts that the old shortlist would have missed, and whether it avoids selecting pipes that have clearly just been replaced.

### Step two: create the minimum data foundation

Build a single working list, even if it starts small.

The pipe register should contain, as far as possible:

- section identifier,
- location geometry,
- material,
- diameter,
- year laid,
- length,
- current status,
- replacement or rehabilitation history.

The burst history should contain, for each recorded burst:

- date or at least month,
- street location,
- coordinates or geocoding,
- whether it was a main burst or another repair type,
- the pipe section it was assigned to, if possible,
- the source work order,
- any cause or follow-up note.

Because your work orders are scanned, you will likely need a staged digitisation process. You do not have to digitise six years before you can learn something. You can start with the most recent complete year, and the prior year, to test whether the method works.

### Step three: choose the matching unit and accept uncertainty

If the burst cannot be matched to a single section, do not force it. Create a confidence flag:

- confident match to a section,
- confident match to a street block but not a section,
- uncertain match.

Uncertain records should not be discarded immediately, but they should not silently pollute the model. Later you can decide whether to improve them with site visits, repair crew knowledge, or mapping fixes.

### Step four: define the historical period and the test period

With six years of records, use time order. That is important. Do not shuffle the years.

Possible structure:

- use earlier burst history to build the score,
- use the later year or two to test whether the score identified sections that actually burst,
- compare the later-year bursts against the sections selected by the old rule and by the new score.

This creates a fair backtest. You are asking: if we had only used the older information, would the new method have produced a better 18 km replacement list for the future period?

### Step five: build the first simple score

Use only fields you can trust.

A practical starting score can combine:

- recent burst density, measured in a comparable way for pipes of different lengths,
- older burst density, to catch long-run behaviour,
- year laid, so older pipes are not treated the same as newer ones,
- material type, if the register shows known problematic materials,
- diameter category, because large-diameter failures often matter more operationally,
- exclusion or downweighting of sections that were recently replaced, unless the data clearly show the record belongs to a different section.

The score should be transparent. You should be able to say why a section ranks high: because it burst recently, because it is old and in a bad material class, because it is large diameter, or because several of these apply.

### Step six: test the new score against the old method

Create two replacement shortlists for the test period:

- the old shortlist: streets with the most past bursts,
- the new shortlist: highest-scored pipe sections or blocks, selected until the 18 km budget is filled.

Then compare them with the actual bursts in the test period.

Look at:

- how many actual bursts fall inside the selected replacement length,
- whether the new shortlist finds bursts that the old shortlist misses,
- whether the new shortlist avoids obviously already-replaced or low-risk sections,
- whether the ranking changes only slightly, which would mean the old rule was already doing the work,
- whether the changes are mostly driven by poor geocoding, which would mean data is the bottleneck.

The key question is not “does this model have a high score?” It is “does this produce a better replacement plan than the current rule?”

### Step seven: add expert and operational review

Model output should not directly replace your judgement. Asset managers, field crews, and operations staff can see things data cannot:

- streets where burst repairs are easy or cheap, so failures appear more often,
- areas where leaks are misreported as bursts,
- newly replaced sections with stale records,
- sections with poor access where bursts cause unusually large disruption,
- hydraulic sensitivity,
- upcoming development or road works.

This review stage also protects against the model chasing historical reporting artefacts.

### Step eight: only then consider a statistical model

If the simple ranking works, and the data quality is adequate, move to a statistical model. At that point you can estimate whether, for example, certain material and age combinations burst more often than would be expected from burst counts alone.

Use the statistical model to improve ranking, not to produce probabilities you do not need yet. The business question is selection under a replacement constraint, so the model should support choosing a list, not just assigning abstract risk numbers.

### Step nine: consider consequences only after likelihood has a data basis

If later you find that some bursts are far more damaging than others, then add consequence weighting. But do not let consequence estimates become the first layer of subjectivity. It is much easier to check whether a pipe is likely to burst than to prove that a burst there would be more harmful than a burst elsewhere.

## When to stop or change course

Stop the modelling work and fix the data if:

- bursts cannot be confidently matched to pipe sections,
- the pipe register contains many missing or contradictory attributes,
- the simple score produces selections that field staff immediately reject as nonsense,
- the backtest shows the new shortlist is no better than the old method,
- apparent improvements are driven only by a few streets with unusual reporting history.

Continue and refine if:

- a decent share of bursts can be matched to sections,
- the simple score ranks known problematic pipes more sensibly than raw burst counts,
- the backtest shows it would have selected sections that actually burst,
- users understand and accept the logic,
- the method gives you better confidence in the annual 18 km choice.

## My direct answer

This is worth doing, but the first deliverable is not a sophisticated model. The first deliverable is a defensible pipe-section failure evidence base and a simple ranking method. That is the foundation that lets you answer the real question: whether replacing 18 km based on your new evidence would be better than replacing 18 km based on the old “most bursts” rule. If it does, then you build on it. If it does not, you have learned that your current method is already doing most of the work, or that the data are too weak to support anything else.

transcript.text: I am the academic director of a group of four private secondary schools. Last year 19 percent of our 1,150 final-year pupils failed the national maths exam in June. This year we can pay for extra tutoring for 120 pupils, starting in October. I want to predict which pupils are most likely to fail, so the places go to the right ones. We hold their grades from earlier years, their attendance, and the mock exam they sit in March. I will not share pupil records: they are children, their parents have not consented, and our board's policy forbids it. Tell me how you would do this without seeing them.

# A solution designed without data

## The problem

The decision is which pupils receive the 120 paid tutoring places before the October start. The academic director, with school leaders and the board’s data or safeguarding owner, makes or approves the list. The unit is one final-year pupil in one cohort-year.

Known from what you told me: four private secondary schools; 1,150 final-year pupils this year; last year's reported failure rate for that year group; 120 tutoring places are available; earlier-year grades, attendance, and a March mock exist; pupil records cannot be shared because they are children and consent or policy restricts it.

Not known: whether the allocation list must be frozen in October before the current March mock, how many pupils will fail this year, which historical fields are available for past cohorts, whether past tutoring affected past outcomes, whether the schools differ sharply in size, and whether any support or access needs can lawfully be used or only monitored.

## What needs care

- **No external sharing.** The method must run inside your data environment, or with a contractor who keeps pupil-level records local.
- **The mock may be after the decision.** If the 120 places are allocated in October, the current March mock is known after the decision and cannot be an input to that decision.
- **Capacity is below last year's apparent failure load.** Using last year's stated failure signal, the number of failing pupils would have been larger than the 120 places available, but last year's rate cannot be assumed for this year.
- **Labels arrive late.** The true outcome is the June national maths result, known only after the allocation decision.
- **Tutoring changes outcomes.** If past supported pupils were selected because they were already risky, historical labels may reflect tutoring, not pure risk.
- **Four-school fairness matters.** A purely global list may leave some schools uncovered if school sizes, grades, or attendance records differ.

## Options

1. **No model: manual risk list.**  
   Cost: staff time to extract local fields and apply a simple rule.  
   Gives: an immediate, explainable way to fill 120 places.  
   Weakness: may miss combinations of grades, attendance, and test history; still has to choose among 1,150 pupils.

2. **Local, privacy-preserving model using pre-October data.**  
   Cost: internal analyst or contracted technical help; governance review; pseudonymous data table.  
   Gives: a ranked risk list using historical patterns, without sharing records outside the schools.  
   This is the option I choose because it directly answers the request for prediction and can be done without pupil-level records leaving your system.

3. **Delay the main decision until after the March mock.**  
   Cost: tutoring may start later or the October places may be provisional.  
   Gives: the strongest available maths signal before the June exam.  
   Weakness: it does not fit “extra tutoring starting in October” unless you use a two-stage list: provisional October places plus March adjustments.

4. **Send data to an external vendor.**  
   Cost: likely requires consent, legal approval, and risk of breach.  
   Gives: outside modelling capacity.  
   Loses because your board policy and children's privacy constraints forbid it.

5. **Build a fake-data demonstration.**  
   Cost: limited.  
   Gives: a rehearsal only.  
   Loses because it cannot decide who gets the real 120 places and cannot tell you whether your real risk factors work.

## Business solution

Start now with a manual list that can run inside each school without any model or external sharing.

Action: freeze a local risk register for the final-year pupils, using only fields already held before the allocation date: prior maths grades, prior attendance, and any maths test score completed before the allocation date.

Simple rule: mark a pupil as a priority candidate if:

- their most recent prior maths grade is below your school's historical failing band or internal pass threshold; or
- their attendance in the latest complete year is below the school's normal expectation; or
- they have both a weak prior maths grade and weak attendance.

Then rank candidates within each school from the most adverse evidence to the least adverse evidence. Fill the 120 places globally, or if the board wants equal school shares, use `120 / 4 = 30` places per school. If school sizes differ, allocate within each school by risk but do not let one school absorb places purely because its grade coding is different.

Cost: administrative time to produce the local list; the tutoring budget covers exactly the 120 paid places. Gain: the places are targeted at visible risk rather than spread randomly. The gain in pass rates is not yet known because last year's failure signal is only a prior year's failure signal, not a guarantee for this year's 1,150 pupils.

## Data to record

| column | what it is | known when | role |

| pupil_key | deterministic pseudonymous identifier for one final-year pupil in one year | before | key |
| school_id | which of the four schools the pupil belongs to | before | input |
| cohort_year | year the pupil is due to sit the June national maths exam | before | time |
| decision_date | date when the 120 tutoring places are frozen | at | time |
| prior_internal_maths_score_1 | most recent maths internal score available before the allocation decision | before | input |
| prior_internal_maths_score_2 | second most recent maths internal score available before the allocation decision | before | input |
| entry_maths_grade | maths grade at entry to secondary school, if available before allocation | before | input |
| attendance_percent_last_complete_year | attendance percentage for the last complete school year before allocation | before | input |
| attendance_percent_to_decision_date | attendance percentage up to the allocation date | at | input |
| maths_test_before_allocation | any maths test score taken before the allocation date, excluding this year's March mock if allocation is in October | before | input |
| support_or_access_need_documented | documented access or support need, recorded only if lawful and necessary for service delivery; not used as a model input unless explicitly approved | before | not used |
| assigned_tutoring_place | whether the pupil was allocated one of the 120 places | at | not used |
| final_maths_exam_fail | official result: the pupil failed the June national maths exam | after | label |
| current_march_mock_score | this year's March mock score, when the October allocation decision is earlier | after | not used |

## Model

Use a local ranking model built inside your data environment. The target is not “attendance risk” or “mock risk”; it is failure in the June national maths exam.

First baseline: rank pupils by the most recent prior maths score only, from lowest to highest; break ties by the lowest attendance-to-decision date score. This baseline is easy to audit and should be the comparison model.

Include school effects so one school's grading habits do not dominate the model. If the number of labelled historical pupils is large enough and relationships appear non-linear, compare with a regularised gradient-boosted tree model; if it does not beat logistic regression, use logistic regression.

Training and testing: train on earlier final-year cohorts where the June outcome is known. Split by school-year, for example leave one school-year out for validation at a time, or train on older years and test on the most recent complete year. Do not use random splits only, because they can hide drift between years and schools.

Measures: rank pupils by predicted failure risk. Use AUC for overall ranking ability, but the decision measure is capacity-based: in a held-out year, how many of the 120 highest-risk pupils actually failed the June exam. 4. **Run the immediate manual rule.** Produce the priority list using existing prior maths grades and attendance. 5. **Assemble historical labels.** For previous final-year cohorts, obtain the June fail/pass outcome and the same pre-decision fields as they would have had before their allocation date. Check: every model feature in historical training rows was available before that historical decision date.

6. **Compare the baseline and local model.** Fit logistic regression on earlier cohorts and validate by school-year. Check: if the model does not beat the baseline on held-out ranking, keep the baseline. If it beats the baseline, use it to produce the next year’s list.

7. **Review fairness across the four schools.** Check: the selected 120 pupils are not concentrated in one school due to grade coding differences, attendance systems, or missing data. Check: each school’s share matches the approved rule.

8. **Score the current cohort locally.** Apply the baseline or validated model to current pupils using only pre-decision fields. Check: the ranked list has 120 names only in the secure school environment, and the external consultant or analyst has no pupil-level output.

- Whether last year's failure signal was stable across all four schools or concentrated in one school.
- Whether prior maths grades, attendance, or pre-decision maths test scores carry real predictive weight once school-level grading differences are removed.

- I assume the pass boundary and grading rules are stable enough that prior-year learning is relevant to this year’s decision, but not guaranteed to transfer perfectly.

## Possible approaches, and what each costs and gives

### No model at all: teacher nominations or existing safety-net rules

You allocate places using head-of-department judgment, known pupil difficulties, safeguarding information, or existing school rules for pupils already identified as needing support.

- Cost: low. No data processing, no modelling, no external access.
- Gives: quick, defensible as support rather than prediction, and avoids labelling pupils through scores.
- Weakness: it is not a calibrated prediction of June failure; it may favour vocal pupils or stable patterns and miss borderline pupils.

### Simple internal scorecard

Staff assign risk points to earlier grades, attendance, and the mock. For example, lower maths grade bands, poorer attendance, and lower mock results receive more risk points. The ranking is then used to choose pupils.

- Cost: low to moderate. Requires an internal meeting to agree bands and a secure spreadsheet or school system.
- Gives: more consistency than pure judgment, transparent and auditable, no complex modelling.
- Weakness: point weights are guesses unless checked against last year’s results; it can be rigid if a pupil’s circumstances are unusual.

### Locally fitted simple model

Your school staff fit a simple model on last year’s pupil data, using available fields and the pass/fail outcome, then apply it to current pupils. The model remains inside the schools. This could be a simple logistic model or a rank-based score. The aim is not to be fancy; it is to use last year’s known failure pattern to guide selection.

- Cost: moderate. Requires data preparation, a person able to fit a model, secure storage, logging, and governance review.
- Gives: the strongest practical prediction from the fields you have, while still avoiding external sharing of records.
- Weakness: depends on data quality, last year’s comparability, and a lawful internal basis. It must not become an opaque decision-maker.

### Cross-school privacy-preserving learning

The four schools could attempt a method where a shared model is learned without moving individual records, such as federated learning or careful summary aggregation.

- Cost: high. Requires strong technical support, legal review, secure systems, and clear governance.
- Gives: potentially better estimates if one school’s labelled history is sparse.
- Weakness: likely overkill for 120 places, especially when the main constraint is consent and policy.

### Lottery or random allocation with priority rules

You define priority bands, then allocate places by lottery within bands.

- Cost: low.
- Gives: fairness and a defence against claims of hidden bias.
- Weakness: does not identify the highest-risk pupils, so it is weak for the prediction goal.

## Chosen approach: a locally run simple model, with a human review stage

I would choose the locally fitted simple model only if authorised staff can lawfully and securely process pupil data internally. If that lawful basis is not confirmed, the fallback should be the simple internal scorecard or no-model teacher nomination.

The key point is this: I provide the design and checking logic; your schools run the data work inside their own systems. No pupil record needs to reach me.

## How to do it, in order

### Before any data work

Each school should confirm with its senior leadership and data protection oversight that internal use of existing pupil records for academic support is permitted. The purpose should be narrow: allocate tutoring support to pupils at higher risk of failing maths, not to assess teachers, rank pupils permanently, or communicate failure predictions to pupils or parents.

Agree that only named authorised staff can access the data. Keep the work inside a secure school system. Log who accessed what. Do not send individual records outside the schools.

### Define the prediction target and timing

The target is a yes-or-no outcome: failure in the national maths exam in June.

The selection moment is the date when the 120 places must be filled. If that is before the March mock, do not include the current mock. Use earlier grades and attendance, plus any earlier mock that already exists. If places can be reviewed after the March mock, create an updated ranking then. The model must not silently use information that will not be available when the decision is made.

### Prepare the previous-year training set internally

For last year’s final-year pupils, staff should assemble, inside the school system, the available maths-related information and the June pass/fail result. The fields should match what will be available for current pupils at the selection date.

Use only features relevant to maths risk: earlier maths grades or a clear maths grade composite, attendance, and the mock if available at selection time. Avoid background attributes unless they are genuinely necessary, lawful, and reviewed for fairness.

### Build a simple interpretable score

The best practical form is a simple additive risk score. For each pupil, convert each available feature into a risk contribution:

- worse earlier maths grades increase risk;
- worse attendance increases risk;
- a lower mock score increases risk, only if available at selection time.

Staff can learn the weights from last year’s known failures using a simple local model. If the sample or data are too messy for a stable model, staff can instead set the weights by consensus and check them against last year’s results.

If attendance is very irregular, or a pupil has missing data, do not treat missingness as a high-risk signal unless staff deliberately decide that a known absence pattern is relevant. Otherwise use a separate “needs review” path.

### Score the current pupils locally

Each school produces its own internal ranked list of current final-year pupils by risk score. The list should stay inside the school. If you need to allocate the 120 places across schools, you can use non-sensitive school-level counts: how many pupils each school has, how many are in high-risk bands, and last year’s failure distribution across the schools. If that is still too sensitive, each school can allocate its assigned share of the 120 places internally.

The output to use should not be a label saying “this pupil will fail.” It should be a support-priority ranking.

### Add human review

Before places are fixed, maths teachers or pastoral staff should check the top of the list for obvious errors or special circumstances:

- data entry mistakes;
- a pupil whose attendance problem was resolved;
- a pupil with special educational needs requiring a different form of support;
- a pupil recently improved;
- a pupil whose mock was disrupted by illness;
- a pupil already receiving another form of help.

Overrides should be allowed but logged with a reason. This prevents the model from becoming the sole judge of children.

### Allocate the places

Use the reviewed ranking to fill the 120 places. If there are already clear safety-net categories from school practice, apply them first, then fill any remaining places from the highest-risk remaining pupils. Do not create a new category just for the model unless staff agree it improves the result.

## How the result is checked

### Check against last year’s known outcomes

This is the main check, and it can be done without sharing records.

Staff should take last year’s 1,150 pupils, use only the information that would have been available at the selection date, score them, and select the top 120. Then staff count internally how many of those 120 actually failed last year. Compare that with a random draw of 120 pupils from last year’s cohort.

If the model-selected 120 do not capture more known failures than the random draw, the ranking is not useful enough to replace teacher judgment or a scorecard.

### Check the direction and shape of the ranking

Staff should confirm that the highest-risk pupils generally have the pattern expected: weaker maths grades, weaker attendance, and lower mock scores where available. If the model says strong pupils are the highest risk, something is wrong in data preparation or scoring.

### Check school balance

The list should not simply reward one school because of better data completeness or a different mock standard. Staff can review how many pupils from each school are selected and why. If one school is over-represented because of data comparability rather than need, adjust the method or use school-relative rankings.

### Check fairness without overfitting

Review whether pupils from disadvantaged backgrounds or protected groups are being selected mainly because their attendance or grades are affected by circumstances unrelated to support need. If so, use human review, safer categories, or non-pupil attributes only if lawful and necessary.

### Treat this year’s June outcome carefully

After June, you can see whether tutored pupils passed. But this will not cleanly prove the prediction was right, because the tutoring itself may have helped. It is better to use last year’s backtest to judge the prediction step, and this year’s outcomes to judge the overall support system.

## When to stop

Stop the allocation process when the 120 places have been assigned and reviewed.

Stop using the model, or revert to a scorecard or teacher nomination, if any of these happen:

- the internal lawful basis is unclear or denied;
- last year’s backtest does not beat a random draw of 120;
- staff cannot trust the ranking because data quality is poor;
- the model gives strange results that teachers reject;
- it creates unfair patterns across schools or pupil groups;
- pupils or parents begin to see the score as a prediction of failure rather than support need.

Before the next year, do a short review: did the method help, were the places used, and did the validation hold? If the answer is weak, simplify the method.

## What I can deliver without seeing records

I cannot give you names, scores, or a pupil list. I can give you this method, the validation checks, and a process your schools can run internally. You should receive assurance rather than pupil records: confirmation that the lawful basis was checked, that last year’s backtest was done, that the 120 places were filled, and that human review was applied.

A final practical warning: do not communicate these results as “most likely to fail.” Communicate them as “highest priority for maths support.” That matters for children, parents, teachers, and the credibility of the tutoring programme.
